prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling atomic frequency standards with uncertainties at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery-grade advance in measurement. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between many-atom statistics and motional and light-shift perturbations, and Ye's work turned that idea into clocks with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and coherence times that open a many-body regime. The result is reproduced with Sr, Yb and other species in many laboratories, compared across continents, and is already used in tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the preparation for redefining the second. The attribution fits two names cleanly: one proposer-and-first-demonstrator, one who carried the platform to record accuracy. Among the shortlisted entries it has the broadest support in the opening ballots (three first places, six top-three rankings, ranked by all eight members) and, unlike most of the others, no credit-allocation crisis forces a hard exclusion.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. Hall and Hansch (frequency combs, 2005) and Wineland (single-ion control, 2012) already cover the comb and ion-clock lineages, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the next incremental step in optical frequency metrology. The practical redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the societal consequence is still prospective. Other groups (Lemonde, the PTB, NIST and Paris clocks, Ido and Takamoto) contributed to the early lattice-clock record and sit outside the two credited names.

responses.point: Ranks B001 first on precision-physics grounds and flags whether the committee sees it as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, along with unresolved roles of other early lattice-clock groups.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and share the worry. I would answer it on scientific content: the 2005 prize rewarded a ruler for optical frequency and the 2012 prize rewarded control of one quantum system. The lattice clock is a different solution to the stability problem, since it interrogates many atoms at once while keeping the atoms in a state-insensitive trap. I do not think that is merely incremental. I also accept that the early-credit question is not fully settled and that Katori, rather than any later group, should anchor the citation.

responses.point: Puts B013 first on the theory-plus-experiment pairing of the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 discovery, calls recognition timely, and ranks B001 fifth citing his limited metrology expertise.
responses.response: I take the B013 case seriously and have moved it up in my own thinking, because the prediction was confirmed by experiment in a way that created a field. My disagreement is about robustness of the record rather than quality. For B013 the pairing mechanism is still debated and Andrei's role remains a live credit problem that the three-person limit cannot absorb. For B001 the observable is the clock accuracy itself, which has been verified by independent comparisons and has no comparable interpretive ambiguity. I understand that metrology is outside your area, and I would invite you to test the 1e-18 claim against the independent comparison record rather than discount it.

responses.point: Places B024 first for the quantum spin Hall proposal and HgTe realisation and ranks B001 fifth, noting that the redefinition of the second is pending and that the case may read as an extension of 2005.
responses.response: I accept that topological insulators are a conceptual change of the first order and that the field is mature and arguably overdue. My reservation is on the cut of credit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Hasan and Mele cannot all be accommodated within three names, and any trio will read as arbitrary to part of the community. On the pending redefinition, I would not make the prize conditional on a metrological body vote; the discovery stands on demonstrated accuracy. Where I partly concede is that Hall's connection to the earlier prize does make B001 look more like a continuation than I first said, and the citation should be worded around the lattice, not around frequency metrology generally.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first while placing B001 second, and states plainly that overlap with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize may lead colleagues to see it as too close to recent recognition.
responses.response: I respect that you disclosed your own proximity to the field. I agree the 2025 award does not remove cQED as a distinct invention, but I think it lowers its priority this year more than the overlap with 2005 and 2012 lowers B001, because the circuit prize is much closer in domain and in recency, and Devoret's role in both makes the credit sensitive. I would put cQED among the alternatives but not in front of the clock.

responses.point: Ranks B001 first on the strength of precise atomic-structure control, but asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second and whether lattice clocks are sufficiently distinct from the single-ion tradition.
responses.response: Your point that the systematics rest on careful atomic-structure inputs (polarisabilities, blackbody and relativistic shifts) is exactly why I regard this as hard physics and not engineering. On waiting, I disagree: the discovery is the demonstrated uncertainty, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that may follow later by years. On the single-ion tradition, the two approaches are competitive and complementary, and the lattice clock's many-atom statistics gave a different route to 1e-18 stability, which I think justifies a separate prize rationale.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
The priority chronology between early lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations beyond Katori and Ye, and the roles of Lemonde and other groups, which I have not independently verified.
Whether a prize that cites only two laureates leaves out contributors in a way that colleagues would find unfair.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during my doctoral period. Hall is not a candidate, but his 2005 prize on optical frequency combs is the closest prior-prize lineage to B001, so I disclose it as a personal connection that could bear on how I weigh distinctness. I have no documented relationship with Katori or Ye. My Lund atomic-physics and quantum-memory work is adjacent to B041 and B046, so I would discount my enthusiasm for those entries, and I have no other specific conflict apparent from my profile.
